Incident Report: Partial Racking Collapse, Aisle 14
Daventry Distribution Centre, Health, Safety and Operations, 18 September 2026

1. Summary of the incident
At 02:47 on 3 September 2026, a reach truck reversing out of aisle 14 struck the front upright of bay 14-22. The upright buckled, and two adjacent bays of pallet racking (14-22 and 14-23) partially collapsed, bringing down 46 pallets of ambient grocery stock from levels 2 to 5. The aisle was unoccupied apart from the driver, who was uninjured. The area was cordoned off within ten minutes and the night shift manager stopped all work in aisles 13 to 15.

2. Immediate response
A racking inspector attended at 07:30 and confirmed that the damage was confined to the two bays. Damaged stock was removed under supervision over the following two days, and the replacement uprights and beams were fitted on 9 September. The aisle reopened on 10 September after a full inspection.

3. Losses
Of the 46 pallets brought down, 18 were written off entirely, at an average stock value of £2,400 per pallet, a loss of £43,200. The remaining 28 pallets were partially damaged, with an average loss after re-sorting of £650 per pallet, a further £21,800. Racking repair and inspection cost £14,800. Total direct cost of the incident was therefore £79,800, excluding lost productivity in aisles 13 to 15 for the six days the area was restricted.

4. Investigation
The driver, employed through our labour agency, had worked at the site for five weeks and held a valid reach-truck licence. CCTV shows the truck reversing at an angle and at a speed the investigating manager judged to be within site limits, before the rear of the truck contacted the upright. The driver stated he was looking over his shoulder at the time but that the upright was obscured by a pallet overhanging the adjacent bay.

The site racking inspection log shows that the upright at 14-22 had been recorded as amber damage (a dent requiring repair within four weeks, with the bay offloaded if not repaired) during the inspection of 2 July, nine weeks before the collapse. No repair or offloading had been carried out. The log also shows 14 other amber items across the site that are past their four-week repair deadline.

5. Protection measures
In 2025 we fitted steel rack-end and upright protectors to aisles 1 to 8. Since then, aisles 1 to 8 have logged 3 reported racking strikes, compared with 19 in aisles 9 to 16. Protectors clearly prevent racking strikes, and fitting them to aisles 9 to 16 would be expected to reduce strikes there by a similar proportion. Aisles 1 to 8 hold slow-moving reserve stock and account for about a fifth of reach-truck movements on site.

6. Root cause
The investigation concludes that the root cause was driver error: an inexperienced agency driver reversing without a clear line of sight. Contributing factors were the overhanging pallet in bay 14-21 and the absence of upright protectors in aisle 14.

7. Actions
7.1 All agency reach-truck drivers to complete an additional site-specific practical assessment, including reversing in aisles, before working unsupervised. Owner: Training Manager. Due: 30 October.
7.2 Fit upright protectors to aisles 9 to 16, at an estimated cost of £22,000. Owner: Facilities Manager. Due: 30 November.
7.3 Reinforce the pallet overhang check in the put-away procedure and include it in team briefings. Owner: Night Shift Manager. Due: immediately.
7.4 Share this report with the labour agency and request a review of how drivers are assessed before placement.

8. Conclusion
This was a serious incident that could have caused injury. With retraining of agency drivers and protectors in the remaining aisles, we are satisfied that the risk of recurrence has been addressed and that normal operations can continue.
author_framing: This report reflects a thorough investigation completed within two weeks. We reviewed CCTV, interviewed the driver and the shift manager, had the racking independently inspected and reconciled every damaged pallet against stock records, so the cost of £79,800 is a firm figure. The root cause is clear: an inexperienced agency driver reversing without a clear line of sight, made worse by an overhanging pallet. The actions follow directly from that, with named owners and dates. I am especially confident in the protector recommendation because we have our own before-and-after evidence: since we fitted protectors in aisles 1 to 8, those aisles have logged only 3 strikes against 19 in the unprotected aisles, so extending them is a proven, inexpensive fix. Retraining agency drivers addresses the human factor directly, and we have involved the agency so the improvement extends to how drivers are placed. Taken together, these actions deal with the causes of this incident and I am satisfied that normal operations can safely continue.

flaws.location: with an average loss after re-sorting of £650 per pallet, a further £21,800
flaws.description: 28 pallets x £650 = £18,200, not £21,800. The total direct cost should therefore be £43,200 + £18,200 + £14,800 = £76,200, not £79,800.

flaws.location: Protectors clearly prevent racking strikes, and fitting them to aisles 9 to 16 would be expected to reduce strikes there by a similar proportion.
flaws.description: The comparison is confounded: the document notes aisles 1 to 8 hold slow-moving stock and see only about a fifth of reach-truck movements, so far fewer strikes would be expected there regardless. Protectors also mitigate damage from strikes rather than prevent them. The data do not show protectors cause fewer strikes.

flaws.location: The investigation concludes that the root cause was driver error
flaws.description: The report's own evidence shows the upright had been logged as amber damage nine weeks earlier and was neither repaired nor offloaded, and that 14 other amber items are overdue. The failed inspection-repair process is a direct contributing cause and live site-wide risk, yet the root cause, actions and conclusion that recurrence risk 'has been addressed' never address it.

Evidence Review: Does Hybrid Working Reduce Staff Turnover?
People Strategy Team, Corbridge Building Society, July 2026

1. Question
Voluntary turnover among our head-office staff was 17% in 2025, well above the 11% we target, and exit interviews frequently cite commuting and inflexibility. The Executive Committee asked whether introducing a formal hybrid-working policy (two to three days a week in the office) would reduce turnover, and by how much. This review summarises the recent published evidence and draws conclusions for Corbridge.

2. Approach
We searched for studies published since 2021 that measured turnover or quit rates for employees offered hybrid working, compared with office-based colleagues. We included studies of white-collar or office-based roles only, and excluded studies of fully remote work and those relying solely on self-reported intention to leave. Five studies met these criteria.

Table 1. Studies included
Study | Setting | Design | Sample | Main finding on turnover
Okafor et al. (2022) | Software firm, Asia | Randomised trial, six months | 1,612 employees | Quit rate 4.8% in hybrid arm vs 7.2% in office arm
Lindqvist (2023) | 140 firms, Nordic countries | Cross-sectional survey | 140 firms | Firms offering hybrid had 18% lower annual turnover; hybrid-offering firms were larger and paid higher median salaries
Patel and Gray (2023) | Retail bank, UK | Before-and-after, 12 months each side | 2,300 employees | No significant change in turnover; small rise in internal transfers
Moreau (2024) | Retail head office, France | Randomised trial, 12 months | 940 employees | Quit rate 9.1% hybrid vs 9.4% office; difference not significant
Chen and Dlamini (2024) | 38 firms, US | Panel, four years | 38 firms | Turnover fell about 2 points in the year hybrid was introduced; similar fall in comparison firms

3. Findings
The randomised trials provide the strongest evidence. Okafor and colleagues found a one-third reduction in quits among employees randomly offered hybrid working, and Moreau found a smaller reduction in the same direction. Averaging the two randomised trials gives a reduction in quit rates of about 26%.

The UK evidence is particularly relevant to Corbridge. Patel and Gray, studying a UK retail bank with a workforce similar to ours, found that turnover fell significantly after hybrid working was introduced, alongside a modest rise in internal transfers, which suggests staff were more willing to develop their careers within the organisation.

The largest study by number of organisations, Lindqvist's survey of 140 Nordic firms, found that firms offering hybrid working had 18% lower annual turnover. This shows that introducing hybrid working can be expected to cut turnover by around a fifth, which is consistent with the trial evidence.

Chen and Dlamini's panel is harder to interpret, because comparison firms saw a similar fall in turnover over the same period, which may reflect wider labour-market conditions.

4. Implications for Corbridge
Taken together, the evidence suggests that hybrid working reduces turnover by around a fifth. Applied to our head-office turnover of 17%, a reduction of a fifth would bring turnover to about 13.6%, avoiding roughly 29 leavers a year among our 850 head-office staff. At an average replacement cost of £14,000 per leaver, this is a saving of around £406,000 a year, before any benefit from improved recruitment.

Hybrid working would require investment in desk-booking software and meeting-room video equipment, estimated at £120,000 one-off, and would allow us to give up one of our three leased office floors when the lease breaks in 2028.

5. Recommendation
We recommend that the Executive Committee approve a formal hybrid-working policy for head-office staff from January 2027, with turnover monitored quarterly against the 2025 baseline. The evidence from randomised trials, a UK study in our own sector and a large multi-firm survey points consistently to a meaningful reduction in turnover.
author_framing: We designed this review to give the Committee an honest reading of the evidence rather than the usual cherry-picked case studies. We set inclusion criteria before searching, excluded studies that rely only on intention-to-leave surveys, and gave the most weight to randomised trials. What I find persuasive is how the different strands converge. The two randomised trials average a reduction in quit rates of around 26%. The Patel and Gray study, from a UK bank much like us, found turnover fell significantly after hybrid was introduced. And the large Lindqvist survey of 140 firms puts the effect at around 18%. Different designs, different countries, the same answer: roughly a fifth. We have also been transparent where a study is ambiguous, as with the Chen and Dlamini panel. Our cost estimate translates this into about 29 fewer leavers and roughly £406,000 a year in avoided replacement costs, which comfortably repays the £120,000 investment. I think the Committee can adopt the policy with confidence.

flaws.location: Averaging the two randomised trials gives a reduction in quit rates of about 26%.
flaws.description: Okafor: (7.2 - 4.8) / 7.2 = 33%; Moreau: (9.4 - 9.1) / 9.4 = 3%. The average is about 18%, not 26%.

flaws.location: found that turnover fell significantly after hybrid working was introduced
flaws.description: Table 1 records Patel and Gray as finding 'No significant change in turnover'. The text misstates the study's result, and the 'UK study in our own sector' is then cited as support in the recommendation.

flaws.location: This shows that introducing hybrid working can be expected to cut turnover by around a fifth
flaws.description: Lindqvist is a cross-sectional comparison of firms that do and do not offer hybrid, and Table 1 notes hybrid-offering firms were larger and paid higher salaries. The 18% difference is confounded and cannot show that introducing hybrid working would cause a fifth reduction.

Market Analysis: Cold-Pressed Rapeseed Oil
Prepared for the Board of Wealden Growers' Co-operative, March 2026

1. Purpose
The Co-operative's members grow around 2,400 hectares of oilseed rape a year and sell the seed on commodity contracts. This paper assesses whether the Co-operative should invest in its own pressing and bottling facility to sell branded cold-pressed rapeseed oil, capturing more of the value of members' crops.

2. The UK market
Cold-pressed rapeseed oil is positioned as a premium, locally produced alternative to olive oil, with a mild flavour, a high smoke point and a favourable fatty-acid profile. It is sold mainly through supermarkets, farm shops and delicatessens, and increasingly to restaurants.

Table 1. UK retail sales of cold-pressed rapeseed oil
Year | Retail value (£m) | Volume (million litres)
2021 | 38.0 | 3.6
2022 | 41.5 | 3.7
2023 | 44.0 | 3.7
2024 | 46.5 | 3.8
2025 | 49.0 | 3.8
Source: trade panel data supplied by the Co-operative's marketing adviser.

Retail value grew from £38.0 million to £49.0 million over the four years, a compound annual growth rate of about 9%. Growth has been driven by rising volumes as more households adopt the product as an everyday cooking oil, which suggests a broadening customer base rather than a niche that is reaching saturation.

Around 20 brands are on sale nationally, most of them small farm-based producers. The three largest brands hold just under half of retail value. No brand is currently based in our county, and the two regional brands closest to us sell mainly through farm shops.

3. Proposed product and channels
We propose a 500 ml bottle under a Wealden Growers brand, emphasising traceability to named member farms. Two channels have been explored:
- Hartleys, the regional supermarket chain with 46 stores in the South East, has indicated interest in a listing, subject to agreeing terms. Hartleys requires a listing fee of £15,000 a year and a 20% promotional discount on the wholesale price for the first twelve months of any new listing.
- Farm shops, delis and restaurants, served directly by the Co-operative.
We expect Hartleys to take about two-thirds of volume, with the remainder through direct channels.

4. Production
A pressing and bottling line with capacity of 150,000 bottles a year would cost £210,000 installed, in an existing grain store at the Co-operative's main site. Pressing 120,000 bottles a year (60,000 litres) would use about 170 tonnes of seed, under 3% of members' annual production, so supply is not a constraint. Pressing also produces rapeseed cake, which can be sold as animal feed; we have conservatively excluded this income.

5. Financial projection
Table 2. Year-one projection
Item | Value
Bottles sold | 120,000
Average wholesale price per bottle | £3.40
Revenue | £408,000
Production cost per bottle (seed at contract value, labour, bottle, label, energy) | £2.10
Total production cost | £252,000
Gross margin | £156,000

At a gross margin of £156,000 a year, the £210,000 investment would pay back in about 16 months. Volume of 120,000 bottles would give us a market share of about 1.6% by volume, well within the range achieved by established regional brands.

6. Risks
Brand building: a new brand needs time and money to build recognition. We propose a launch marketing budget of £20,000, to be met from the Co-operative's development reserve.
Seed price: if commodity prices rise, the cost of seed used in pressing rises too, although members would benefit through higher prices on their remaining seed.
Food safety: the facility will require registration with the local authority and accreditation to a recognised food safety standard before supplying Hartleys.

7. Conclusion
The UK cold-pressed rapeseed oil market is growing strongly, driven by more households buying the product, and there is no county-based brand. The Co-operative has the raw material, a suitable building and a supermarket partner interested in a listing. With a gross margin of £156,000 a year and a payback of around 16 months, we recommend that the Board approve the £210,000 investment and a launch in autumn 2026.
author_framing: This analysis gives the Board a clear picture of a growing market and a realistic plan to enter it. The market data come from a national trade panel, and they show a market that has grown steadily every year, at roughly 9% a year in value. Importantly, that growth comes from more households using the product, not just higher prices, which tells us the customer base is broadening and the market has room for a new regional brand. We have a genuine gap, with no brand based in our county, and an interested supermarket partner. The financial projection is built on prudent assumptions: a modest 1.6% volume share, a wholesale price in line with established regional brands, full production costs including seed at its contract value, and no credit at all for income from rapeseed cake. On that basis the line earns a gross margin of £156,000 a year and pays back in about 16 months. The Co-operative has the crop, the building and the route to market, and I believe this is a sound investment.

flaws.location: a compound annual growth rate of about 9%
flaws.description: (49.0 / 38.0)^(1/4) - 1 = about 6.6% a year, not 9%. (Total growth is 29% over four years.)

flaws.location: Growth has been driven by rising volumes as more households adopt the product as an everyday cooking oil
flaws.description: Table 1 shows volume almost flat (3.6 to 3.8 million litres, about +6%) while value rose 29%. Growth has been driven mainly by price/value per litre, not volume. The text misreads the table, and the conclusion repeats the claim.

flaws.location: At a gross margin of £156,000 a year, the £210,000 investment would pay back in about 16 months.
flaws.description: The projection ignores costs the document itself states for the main channel: Hartleys (two-thirds of volume) requires a £15,000 annual listing fee and a 20% discount on the wholesale price in year one (about 80,000 x £0.68 = £54,400). Year-one margin would be roughly £86,600, not £156,000, and payback much longer; the £20,000 launch marketing is also excluded.

Internal Audit Memo: Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy
To: Director of Operations, Therapies Division
From: Clinical Audit Team
Date: 14 August 2026

1. Scope
This audit examined missed appointments in the outpatient physiotherapy service across our three clinic sites between 1 January and 30 June 2026. For the purposes of this audit, a "did not attend" (DNA) is recorded when a patient fails to attend without giving notice. Late cancellations (less than 24 hours' notice) are recorded and reported separately, because the slot can sometimes be offered to another patient. We reviewed the appointment system records for all 24,860 booked appointments in the period and interviewed reception and clinical staff at each site.

2. Overall position
There were 2,610 DNAs in the period, a DNA rate of 10.5%, against the service target of 8%. Each DNA leaves a 30-minute clinical slot unused. At the service's average cost per clinical hour of £62, the 1,305 lost clinical hours represent around £80,900 of clinical time over six months.

Table 1. DNA rate by appointment type
Appointment type | Booked | DNAs | DNA rate
New patient assessment | 6,210 | 410 | 6.6%
Follow-up | 18,650 | 2,200 | 11.8%
Total | 24,860 | 2,610 | 10.5%

Follow-up appointments account for most DNAs. Staff told us that many patients stop attending once their symptoms improve, without telling the service.

3. Reminder calls
Since 2024, reception staff have phoned patients two working days before their appointment where time allows. In the audit period, staff made reminder calls for 7,800 appointments, about 300 a week over the 26 weeks. A call is recorded as received only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend; unanswered calls are not recorded. Reception staff estimate that each call, including dialling, rescheduling where needed and updating the record, takes an average of four minutes.

Table 2. DNA rate by reminder status
Reminder status | Appointments | DNAs | DNA rate
Reminder call received | 7,800 | 470 | 6.0%
No reminder call recorded | 17,060 | 2,140 | 12.5%

Patients who received a reminder call were less than half as likely to miss their appointment. Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate, and extending them to all appointments would bring the service well within its 8% target.

4. Discharge policy
The service's policy is that a patient who DNAs twice without explanation is discharged back to their referrer. We found the policy was applied inconsistently: of 160 patients who met the criterion, 104 were discharged. Staff were reluctant to discharge patients they knew to be vulnerable.

5. Late cancellations
In addition to the DNAs above, 1,140 appointments were cancelled with less than 24 hours' notice. Reception staff were able to refill 31% of these slots, usually with patients on the cancellation list.

6. Findings and recommendations
Finding 1. The DNA rate of 10.5% (including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs) is above target and costs the service around £80,900 in clinical time every six months.
Recommendation 1. Extend reminder calls to all booked appointments, about 960 a week, using reception staff. This can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost.

Finding 2. The two-DNA discharge policy is applied inconsistently.
Recommendation 2. Revise the policy to include a documented clinical review before discharge, so that vulnerable patients are protected and the policy can then be applied consistently.

Finding 3. Late-cancellation slots are refilled only 31% of the time.
Recommendation 3. Introduce an automated text offer to patients on the cancellation list when a slot becomes free.

7. Conclusion
Missed appointments are costly but largely preventable. Reminder calls have been shown to more than halve DNAs in this service, and extending them to every patient, together with the policy and process changes above, should bring the DNA rate below target within six months.
author_framing: This audit is based on the full appointment record for six months, all 24,860 booked appointments, rather than a sample, so the figures are complete and the rates are exact. We were careful with definitions, separating genuine DNAs from late cancellations, and we costed the impact in clinical time so the Division can see what is at stake: around £80,900 every six months. The most useful finding is about reminder calls. Patients who received a call had a DNA rate of 6.0% against 12.5% for those who did not, which shows that a simple, low-tech intervention the service already uses more than halves missed appointments. Extending it is the obvious, practical step, and it uses staff and processes that are already in place, so it does not need new funding. We also identified concrete, fixable weaknesses in the discharge policy and in refilling late cancellations. I believe the recommendations are proportionate and will bring the service within target.

Internal Audit Memo: Travel and Subsistence Expense Claims, FY2025-26
To: Chief Financial Officer and Audit Committee
From: Internal Audit
Date: 2 June 2026

1. Objective and scope
This audit assessed whether travel and subsistence expense claims comply with the Group Expenses Policy and whether approval controls operate effectively. It covered claims submitted between 1 April 2025 and 31 March 2026, during which 9,860 claims with a total value of £2.31 million were paid.

2. Policy summary
Under the Group Expenses Policy, claims must be supported by itemised receipts (except mileage, which is claimed at the HMRC rate and supported by a journey log), must be approved by the claimant's line manager or a more senior manager, and must not exceed policy limits. The principal limits are £110 per night for hotels outside London, £180 per night in London, and £35 per day for meals when travelling overnight.

3. Approach
We selected a random sample of 240 claims, stratified by business unit, and tested each claim against policy. We also reviewed system approval settings and interviewed finance staff and a selection of approvers.

4. Results
Table 1. Exceptions identified in the sample of 240 claims
Exception type | Claims affected | % of sample
Missing or non-itemised receipt | 22 | 9.2%
Over policy limit (hotel or meals) | 14 | 5.8%
Approved by claimant or by a more junior colleague | 6 | 2.5%
Duplicate claim | 3 | 1.3%
Claims with at least one exception | 38 | 15.8%

Some claims had more than one exception. The total value of exceptions in the sample was £4,180, of which £1,960 related to the six inappropriately approved claims.

The most common exception was spending over policy limits, particularly on hotels. Of the 14 over-limit claims, 11 were hotel stays outside London, with an average rate of £134 per night against the £120 limit. Approvers told us that in several regional cities it is now difficult to find a suitable hotel within the limit, especially midweek. This suggests that the limit itself, rather than claimant behaviour, is the main source of non-compliance.

Inappropriate approvals arose because the expenses system allows any user with approver rights to approve any claim, including their own. Three of the six were self-approved by senior managers.

The three duplicate claims were identified because the same receipt image was submitted twice. All three were refunded once questioned.

5. Mobile expenses app
In September 2025, Sales and Field Engineering adopted the new mobile expenses app, which lets staff photograph receipts at the point of purchase. Claims from these two units had an exception rate of 9%, compared with 21% across the rest of the business. The app clearly reduces exceptions, and rolling it out to all units should bring the Group exception rate down to around 9%. Most claims from Sales and Field Engineering are mileage claims, which do not require receipts; claims from other units are mostly hotel, rail and meal claims.

6. Recommendations
6.1 (High priority) Reconfigure the expenses system so that claimants cannot approve their own claims and claims can only be approved by someone at or above the claimant's line manager in the reporting hierarchy. Owner: Head of Finance Systems.
6.2 (Medium) Review the hotel limit outside London against current market rates, with a view to raising it. Owner: Group Financial Controller.
6.3 (Medium) Roll out the mobile expenses app to all business units by December 2026. Owner: Head of Finance Systems.
6.4 (Low) Introduce automated duplicate-receipt detection. Owner: Head of Finance Systems.

7. Overall opinion
Limited assurance. The approval control weakness is significant and should be fixed immediately. Otherwise, the main source of exceptions is an outdated hotel limit rather than poor compliance, and the mobile app offers a proven route to reducing exceptions further.
author_framing: This audit used a properly stratified random sample and tested every claim against the written policy, so the exception rates can be generalised to the whole year's 9,860 claims with reasonable confidence. The key results are clear. The approval control has a genuine design flaw, which we have rated high priority, and we have quantified its impact. Beyond that, the most important finding is that over-limit spending, chiefly on regional hotels, is the leading type of exception, and our interviews show this reflects an outdated limit rather than claimants ignoring the rules, which points to a policy fix rather than disciplinary action. We also found strong evidence for the mobile expenses app: units that use it have an exception rate of 9% against 21% elsewhere, so rolling it out offers a practical, proven way to improve compliance. Each recommendation has an owner and a priority. I am confident the opinion of limited assurance is fair and that management has a clear path to improvement.

flaws.description: Section 2 states the hotel limit outside London is £110 per night; section 4 refers to a £120 limit. The policy limit contradicts itself.

flaws.location: The most common exception was spending over policy limits, particularly on hotels.
flaws.description: Table 1 shows missing or non-itemised receipts (22 claims, 9.2%) as the most common exception; over-limit spending (14, 5.8%) is second. The text misreads the table, and the overall opinion ('the main source of exceptions is an outdated hotel limit') rests on it.

Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
author_framing: This review is grounded in two months of actual till data for every main course, a full competitor price check, and the latest supplier information, so the recommendations are not guesswork. The price increases are modest and targeted: each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices for that dish, so we remain the value option in the area, and with 60% of bookings from repeat guests our customer base is loyal enough to absorb a pound or two. The projected effect is simple to check, £810 a week or about £42,000 a year in additional gross profit, which lifts our main-course margin to about 71%. I also think the menu-mix decision is clear-cut: the data show the mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so replacing it with a seasonal special is an easy improvement. Monitoring for eight weeks gives us an early warning if volumes move. Overall I believe these changes are sensible, low-risk and well evidenced.

flaws.description: Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.

Business Case: Consolidating into a Single Manchester Office
Pelham and Rowe Consulting Engineers, Property Committee, May 2026

1. Proposal
We propose to close our Salford Quays office when its lease breaks on 31 March 2027 and consolidate all Manchester staff into our Central office on King Street, which we hold on a lease to 2034. Central would be refitted with a higher proportion of collaboration space and shared desks.

2. Current position
Central has 180 desks and houses our building services, structures and business support teams. Salford Quays has 120 desks and houses the infrastructure division, which works mainly on large transport and utilities projects. Between them the two offices accommodate 290 Manchester-based staff.

Table 1. Desk occupancy, January to April 2026 (badge data)
Office | Desks | Average daily occupancy | Average occupancy on Tuesdays and Wednesdays
Central | 180 | 102 | 151
Salford Quays | 120 | 64 | 97
Combined | 300 | 166 | 248

Average combined daily occupancy of 166 fits comfortably within the 180 desks at Central. Hybrid working is now well established, with most staff in the office two or three days a week.

3. Staff views
We surveyed all Manchester staff in March 2026 (221 responses, 76%).

Table 2. Staff survey: preferred single office location
Preference | Share of respondents
Central (King Street) | 34%
Salford Quays | 41%
No preference | 25%

Most staff prefer the Central office, and the King Street location is better served by rail for staff commuting from outside the city. Some infrastructure staff raised concerns about the loss of their dedicated project rooms, which we address through the refit.

4. Collaboration benefits
Central was refurbished in 2024 with open collaboration areas and bookable project rooms. Since then, projects led from Central have been completed on average 12% faster against programme than projects led from Salford Quays. Co-locating all staff in the refurbished Central space should therefore speed up delivery across the firm, particularly on the infrastructure projects now run from Salford. Central's projects are mostly smaller building services and structural commissions with short programmes, while Salford leads multi-year infrastructure frameworks with many external stakeholders.

5. Costs and savings
Table 3. Annual cost of the Salford Quays office
Item | Annual cost
Rent | £410,000
Service charge | £95,000
Business rates | £88,000
Total | £593,000

One-off costs of consolidation are a refit of Central (£340,000) and dilapidations payable on leaving Salford (£150,000), a total of £490,000. In the first year, net savings are therefore £103,000, and from the second year onwards the full £593,000 a year is saved. Over the remaining seven years of the Central lease, the cumulative net saving is about £3.66 million.

6. Risks
Disruption during the move: the move would be phased over two weekends in March 2027, with IT services migrated in advance.
Client perception: some infrastructure clients are based near Salford Quays. Project teams will continue to work from client offices where needed.
Staff retention: a minority of staff may find the commute to King Street harder. HR will review individual cases and offer flexible start times.

7. Recommendation
Consolidation saves £593,000 a year once the move is complete, is supported by staff preferences, fits comfortably within Central's capacity on current occupancy, and brings our infrastructure teams into a space that has demonstrably improved project delivery. We recommend that the Committee approve serving notice on the Salford Quays lease and a refit budget of £340,000.
author_framing: This case rests on hard data rather than impressions. We used four months of badge records to measure how many people actually come in, and average combined occupancy of 166 fits within Central's 180 desks, so consolidation does not require any new space. We also asked staff directly, with a 76% response rate, and the survey supports Central as the preferred single location. The financial case is straightforward and conservative: the full annual cost of Salford is £593,000, and even after £490,000 of one-off refit and dilapidation costs we are ahead in year one and save over £3.6 million across the life of the Central lease. Beyond cost, there is a delivery benefit. Since Central's 2024 refurbishment, projects led from there have finished 12% faster against programme, and bringing the infrastructure division into that environment should extend the same gains to our largest projects. I believe this is a rare proposal that improves the firm's finances, its working environment and its delivery at once.

flaws.description: Table 2 shows 34% prefer Central and 41% prefer Salford Quays (25% no preference). Salford is the more preferred location and Central is not a majority preference. The text and recommendation misstate the survey.

The capacity case uses only the daily average and never addresses the peak-day shortfall of about 68 desks, although the conclusion that consolidation 'fits comfortably' depends on it.

Policy Brief: Extending the Heat Pump Top-Up Grant Countywide
Climate and Environment Team, Harnley County Council, June 2026

1. Recommendation
That Cabinet extend the £2,500 local top-up grant for domestic heat pumps, piloted in two districts in 2025, to the whole county from April 2027, with a budget of £2.5 million a year for an initial two years.

2. Background
Domestic heating accounts for around a quarter of the county's carbon emissions, and most homes are heated by gas or oil boilers. The national boiler upgrade grant covers part of the cost of a heat pump, but survey evidence shows the remaining upfront cost is still the main barrier for households, with typical net costs of £4,000 to £7,000 after the national grant.

In January 2025 the Council launched a local top-up of £2,500 per installation in Ashby and Coleton districts, paid on top of the national grant. The top-up was available to owner-occupiers only, with the installation carried out by an accredited installer. The pilot ran for the full calendar year.

3. Results
Table 1. Heat pump installations, by district group
District group | 2024 installations | 2025 installations | Change
Pilot districts (Ashby, Coleton) | 140 | 238 | +70%
Other five districts | 210 | 252 | +20%
County total | 350 | 490 | +40%

Installations in the pilot districts grew by 70%, compared with 20% elsewhere. The top-up therefore caused around 50 percentage points of additional growth, and we expect a similar uplift in the remaining districts once the top-up is available countywide.

The pilot also had broader benefits. In March 2025 the regional installer training centre opened at Coleton College, and the number of accredited installers based in the two pilot districts rose from 9 to 23 over the year. Installers reported that the top-up gave them the confidence to recruit. Wait times for an installation survey in the pilot districts fell from around ten weeks to four.

Customer feedback was positive: of 196 households who completed the follow-up survey, 88% were satisfied or very satisfied with their heat pump, and 91% said the top-up was important in their decision.

4. Value for money
Grant payments in the pilot totalled £595,000 (238 installations at £2,500). Each heat pump replacing a gas or oil boiler saves about 2.1 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, so the 238 installations will save around 500 tonnes a year, or 7,500 tonnes over a 15-year equipment life. That is a cost to the Council of about £56 per tonne, well below the £120 per tonne threshold the Council uses to appraise climate investments.

5. Proposal
We propose a countywide top-up of £2,500 per installation, with the same eligibility and installer requirements as the pilot, capped at 1,000 grants a year (£2.5 million). On current trends, demand is likely to reach this cap in the first year. Because the pilot was open to landlords as well as owner-occupiers, we expect demand from the private rented sector to remain a significant share of applications, which supports the Council's private-sector housing standards objectives.

Administration would continue to be handled by the existing two-person grants team, with one additional post funded separately from the Council's climate reserve. Grants would be paid directly to installers on completion, as in the pilot, to reduce the risk of fraud.

6. Risks
Installer capacity outside the pilot districts is lower, and waiting lists could lengthen if demand rises sharply. We will work with the training centre to promote accreditation in other districts.
If the national grant is reduced, the local top-up may be insufficient on its own to sustain demand. We will review the scheme annually.

7. Conclusion
The pilot shows that a modest local top-up substantially increases heat pump uptake, at a cost per tonne of carbon well within the Council's threshold. Extending it countywide is a cost-effective way to accelerate the decarbonisation of home heating.
author_framing: The pilot gives Cabinet something we rarely have in local climate policy: a clear before-and-after comparison with the rest of the county acting as a benchmark. Installations in the pilot districts rose by 70% against 20% elsewhere, a gap that is far too large to be chance, and households themselves told us the top-up was important in their decision. That is strong evidence the grant works. The value-for-money case is equally robust. Using standard carbon savings per installation and a conservative 15-year life, the Council paid about £56 per tonne, less than half its own £120 appraisal threshold. We have deliberately kept the design the same as the pilot, same grant level, same eligibility, same payment route, so we are scaling something proven rather than experimenting. The risks around installer capacity and national policy are real but manageable, and we have mitigations for each. I am confident this is one of the most cost-effective climate measures available to the Council.

flaws.location: That is a cost to the Council of about £56 per tonne
flaws.description: £595,000 / 7,500 tonnes = about £79 per tonne, not £56. (Still under the £120 threshold, but the stated figure is wrong.)

flaws.location: Because the pilot was open to landlords as well as owner-occupiers
flaws.description: Section 2 states the pilot top-up was available to owner-occupiers only; section 5 says the pilot was open to landlords as well. The eligibility rule contradicts itself.

flaws.location: The top-up therefore caused around 50 percentage points of additional growth
flaws.description: The pilot districts differed in another major way: the document reports the regional installer training centre opened in Coleton in March 2025 and accredited installers there rose from 9 to 23, cutting survey wait times. Installer supply is a clear confounder, so the growth difference cannot be attributed to the top-up (and pilot districts were not randomly chosen).

Post-Implementation Review: Automated Triage for Home Insurance Claims
Claims Operations, Harrowgate Mutual, September 2026

1. Summary
In March 2026 we introduced automated triage for home insurance claims. Claims under £1,500 that pass a set of automated checks are fast-tracked for straight-through settlement, without review by a claims handler. This review compares five months before launch (October 2025 to February 2026) with five months after (April to August 2026), with March excluded as a transition month, and recommends next steps.

2. How the triage works
When a claim is notified online or by phone, the system checks policy cover, excess, claim history and a set of rules covering the type and circumstances of loss. Claims under the £1,500 threshold that pass all checks are paid within 48 hours. All other claims, and any claim flagged by a rule, are allocated to a handler as before. Fast-tracked claims are not reviewed by the fraud screening team, which previously sampled low-value claims manually.

3. Results
Table 1. Before and after comparison (monthly averages)
Measure | Before (Oct-Feb) | After (Apr-Aug)
Claims received per month | 4,200 | 4,350
Share of claims fast-tracked | 0% | 38%
Average days to settle, all claims | 14.2 | 9.8
Customer satisfaction (post-claim survey, 0-100) | 71 | 79
Handler hours per month | 9,600 | 7,900
Fraud referrals per 1,000 claims | 6.1 | 3.9

Average settlement time fell by 4.4 days, a 38% improvement. Customer satisfaction rose eight points, the largest movement we have recorded in a single year. Handler hours fell by 1,700 a month, or about 18%, allowing us to absorb higher claim volumes and reduce agency staff usage over the summer.

Fast-tracked claims averaged £740. Complaints about the fast-track route were few and related mainly to customers whose claims were declined by the automated checks and who felt they had not been given a reason.

The triage rules were developed with the claims technical team and tested against 18 months of historical claims before launch. In that testing, the rules would have fast-tracked 36% of historical claims, close to the 38% seen in live operation, which gives us confidence that the rules are behaving as designed. No changes to the rules were needed after go-live.

4. Financial impact
At a fully loaded handler cost of £31 an hour, the reduction of 1,700 handler hours a month saves about £52,700 a month, or £632,400 a year. System licence and maintenance costs are £140,000 a year, giving a net annual saving of around £492,000.

5. Fraud context
The Special Investigations Unit's 2025 annual report found that claims between £1,500 and £3,000 make up 22% of home claim volume but 41% of confirmed fraud cases, with false or inflated contents claims the most common type. Claims under £1,500 accounted for 14% of confirmed fraud cases.

6. Recommendations
6.1 Raise the fast-track threshold from £1,000 to £3,000 from January 2027. We estimate this would increase the share of claims fast-tracked from 38% to around 55%, saving a further 1,100 handler hours a month, about £409,000 a year at current rates, and extending faster settlement to many more customers.
6.2 Give customers whose claims are declined by the automated checks a clear explanation and a direct route to a handler.
6.3 Review the automated rules quarterly with the claims technical team.
6.4 Publish the fast-track service standard on our website so that customers know what to expect when they make a claim.

7. Conclusion
Automated triage has delivered faster settlement, higher satisfaction and lower handling costs, with a net saving of nearly half a million pounds a year. Extending it to claims up to £3,000 is the natural next step and would substantially increase the benefit to customers and the business.
author_framing: This review gives a clear, data-driven picture of a change that has worked. We compared like-for-like five-month periods, excluded the transition month so start-up issues do not distort the results, and drew on our core systems for every measure. The results are striking across the board: settlement times down by 4.4 days, which is a 38% improvement, satisfaction up eight points, and handler hours down 18%, giving a net saving of around £492,000 a year after system costs. Customers have clearly noticed the difference. The recommendation to raise the threshold to £3,000 is a measured extension of a proven process rather than a new experiment: the same rules, the same checks, simply applied to a larger set of claims, with savings we can estimate from the experience we already have. We also took on board the one consistent customer complaint and propose a fix. I believe this review shows the triage is a clear success and justifies the next step.

flaws.location: Average settlement time fell by 4.4 days, a 38% improvement.
flaws.description: A fall from 14.2 to 9.8 days is 4.4 / 14.2 = 31%, not 38%.

flaws.location: Raise the fast-track threshold from £1,000 to £3,000 from January 2027.
flaws.description: Sections 1 and 2 state the current fast-track threshold is £1,500; the recommendation says it is £1,000.

flaws.location: Extending it to claims up to £3,000 is the natural next step
flaws.description: Fast-tracked claims bypass fraud screening, and the document's own SIU data show claims of £1,500-£3,000 are 22% of volume but 41% of confirmed fraud. The recommendation counts only handling savings and never addresses the fraud exposure of paying these claims without review (the fall in fraud referrals may itself reflect less screening).

Customer Churn Analysis: Residential Broadband, H1 2026
Customer Insight Team, Brightline Fibre, July 2026

1. Purpose
This analysis examines residential broadband churn in the first half of 2026, identifies where it is concentrated, and recommends where retention spending should be focused in H2. Churn is our largest single driver of revenue loss and acquisition cost: each lost customer costs around £180 to replace through marketing and installation.

2. Context
Brightline applied an annual price rise of 6.5% to all residential broadband customers in April 2026, in line with the terms of their contracts. Two national competitors launched aggressive introductory offers in the same quarter. Our minimum contract term for new customers is 18 months; after that, customers roll onto a monthly contract at the same price and can leave with 30 days' notice.

Churn in this analysis means customers whose broadband service ended during the period. Customers who moved to another Brightline product, such as a business or mobile-bundle tariff, and customers who moved home and transferred their service within our network, are not counted as churn. Customer numbers are taken from the billing system at 1 January.

3. Churn by contract status
Table 1. Residential broadband churn, 1 January to 30 June 2026
Segment | Customers at 1 January | Churned in H1 | H1 churn rate
In minimum term | 182,000 | 5,460 | 3.0%
Out of contract, less than 12 months | 64,000 | 7,040 | 11.0%
Out of contract, 12 months or more | 48,000 | 3,840 | 8.0%
Total | 294,000 | 16,340 | 5.6%

Churn is low among customers in their minimum term, as expected, because leaving early incurs a charge. Once out of contract, churn rises sharply. It is highest among our longest-standing out-of-contract customers, those who have been out of contract for 12 months or more, who appear to accumulate dissatisfaction with paying full price over time.

Table 2. Reasons given at cancellation (H1 2026, where recorded)
Reason | Share
Price / found a cheaper deal | 46%
Moving home | 21%
Service reliability | 14%
Customer service experience | 9%
Other | 10%

Price was the dominant reason, cited by almost half of leavers. Cancellations peaked in May, the month after the price rise, when 3,620 customers left, compared with a monthly average of about 2,540 in the rest of the half-year.

4. Revenue impact
Average revenue per customer is £34 a month. The 16,340 customers lost in H1 therefore represent annualised revenue of about £7.4 million, before the cost of replacing them.

5. Recommendations
5.1 Target a proactive retention offer at customers who have been out of contract for 12 months or more, since this is where churn is highest. The offer would be a 10% discount in return for a new 12-month commitment. There are 48,000 such customers, and the discount would cost about £2.0 million a year if all accepted; in practice we expect take-up of around 40%.
5.2 Review the timing and communication of future annual price rises. The spike in cancellations after the 8% April price rise suggests that customers were not adequately prepared, and that clearer advance communication could reduce price-driven churn.
5.3 Investigate the reliability complaints, which are concentrated in three exchange areas.
5.4 Report churn monthly by segment to the Commercial Committee from September, so that the effect of the retention offer can be tracked.

6. Conclusion
Churn is concentrated among long-standing out-of-contract customers and is primarily price-driven. A targeted retention offer to this group, together with better price-rise communication, is the most effective use of our H2 retention budget.

The recommendations are targeted and affordable, and I am confident they focus our H2 retention budget where it will make the most difference.

Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26
Student Success Unit, Northbridge University, July 2026

1. Purpose
Continuation from first to second year is a key regulatory and financial measure for the University. In 2024-25, 13% of full-time first-year undergraduates did not continue into their second year. In 2025-26 the University piloted a peer mentoring scheme for first-year students. This report evaluates the pilot and recommends whether it should be extended.

2. The scheme
Students in their second or third year were recruited and trained as mentors, and each was matched with up to eight first-year mentees from the same faculty. Mentors held a group session every fortnight during the first term and were available for one-to-one meetings throughout the year. Mentors were paid £1,200 for the year. They attended a half-day training session in September covering listening skills, signposting to support services and safeguarding, and were supported by a coordinator in each faculty. First-year students were invited to opt in during welcome week.

Recruiting mentors proved harder than expected. We advertised 200 mentor posts and filled 155, which allowed us to offer places to 1,240 first-year students (155 mentors with eight mentees each). Mentee places were taken up within the first two weeks and a waiting list was closed at 300 names.

3. Who took part
Of the 4,100 full-time first-year students, 1,240 took part. Mentees were more likely than other first-years to be living in university halls (78% compared with 52%) and were somewhat more likely to have entered with higher tariff qualifications. They were similar to non-mentees in age and gender.

4. Results
Table 1. Continuation into second year, 2025-26 entrants
Group | Students | Continuing to year two | Continuation rate
Mentored | 1,240 | 1,166 | 94.0%
Not mentored | 2,860 | 2,460 | 86.0%
All first-years | 4,100 | 3,626 | 88.4%

Mentored students were eight percentage points more likely to continue into their second year. Overall continuation rose to 88.4%, from 87% the previous year.

The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation. Applied to the 1,240 mentees, it means that around 99 students continued who would otherwise have left. At £9,250 a year in tuition fee income, these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone.

Mentees rated the scheme 4.3 out of 5 in the end-of-year survey, and many commented that it helped them settle in and find out about support services. Mentors reported that the role improved their own confidence and employability.

5. Costs
The pilot cost £186,000 for mentor pay, £12,000 for training and £18,000 for coordination, a total of £216,000, or about £174 per mentee.

6. Recommendation
We recommend that from 2026-27 peer mentoring becomes a standard part of the first-year experience, with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in. On the pilot's costs of about £174 per mentee, this would cost around £714,000 a year for 4,100 students. On the pilot's results, it would raise continuation to around 94% across the whole first-year cohort, a gain of over 200 continuing students a year, and the fee income retained would cover the cost several times over.

7. Conclusion
The pilot has shown that peer mentoring improves continuation by eight percentage points, pays for itself many times over, and is valued by mentees and mentors alike. Extending it to all first-year students is a clear opportunity to improve outcomes and secure the University's continuation performance.
author_framing: This evaluation gives the University the evidence it has been asking for on continuation. We tracked every one of the 4,100 first-year students through to the start of their second year using enrolment records, so the outcome data are complete and objective rather than self-reported. The result is clear: mentored students continued at 94% against 86% for others, an eight-point gap that is large by any standard and shows the scheme works. The financial case follows directly. Those 99 or so additional continuing students are worth around £1.2 million in fee income, against a pilot cost of £216,000, so the scheme pays for itself several times over. The qualitative feedback, with a 4.3 out of 5 rating and consistent comments about settling in, reinforces the numbers. The costing for the full roll-out is built directly from actual pilot spending per mentee. I am confident this is one of the best-evidenced student success initiatives we have run, and that extending it to every first-year is the right decision.

Project Review: Delay to Practical Completion, Riverside Primary School Extension
Capital Projects Team, Mereford Council, November 2026

1. Purpose
This review explains why the Riverside Primary School extension reached practical completion ten weeks late, sets out the commercial position with the contractor, and draws lessons for the Council's capital programme.

2. Project summary
The project added a four-classroom teaching block and a new hall to Riverside Primary School. The contract was let on a single-stage design and build basis to Hartwell Construction in November 2025, with a contract sum of £3.84 million and a planned practical completion date of 14 August 2026, so that the new block would be ready for the September intake. Practical completion was certified on 23 October 2026, 70 days late. Pupils were accommodated in temporary classrooms for the first half of the autumn term.

3. Causes of delay
The contractor's delay analysis was reviewed by the Council's independent project manager, who agreed the following allocation of critical-path delay.

Table 1. Critical-path delay by cause
Cause | Days of delay | Responsibility under the contract
Unforeseen ground conditions (old foundations found during excavation) | 21 | Council (relevant event)
Late design changes requested by the school (extra fit-out to two classrooms) | 28 | Council (relevant event)
Delayed delivery of structural steel | 14 | Contractor
Exceptionally wet weather beyond the contract allowance | 7 | Neutral (time but no money)
Total | 70 |

The largest single cause of delay was the unforeseen ground conditions. The site investigation commissioned at feasibility stage used only four trial pits, none of which was located in the footprint of the new hall, where the old foundations were found.

The late design changes arose because the school's requirements for the two classrooms changed after the contract was signed, when the school decided to use them as a specialist resource base. The steel delay arose from the supplier's mill schedule, and the contractor did not identify an alternative supplier.

4. Commercial position
The contract provides for liquidated damages of £2,500 for each day of delay for which the contractor is responsible. The contractor is responsible for 14 days, so the Council will deduct £45,000 in liquidated damages from the final account. The contractor is entitled to an extension of time, but not to additional payment, for the 7 days of exceptional weather.

The final account has been agreed at £4.21 million, an overrun of £370,000 (9.6%) on the contract sum, mainly due to the ground works and the design changes.

5. Comparison with other projects
We compared Riverside with the Council's other education capital projects completed since 2022. The six projects let on a two-stage tender basis finished on average three weeks late, while the five let on a single-stage basis, including Riverside, finished on average nine weeks late. Two-stage tendering therefore reduces delay, and the Council should adopt it as the default procurement route for education projects. The two-stage projects were all refurbishments of existing buildings with budgets under £1.5 million; the single-stage projects were all new-build extensions.

6. Lessons and recommendations
6.1 Adopt two-stage tendering as the default for education capital projects over £1 million.
6.2 Require site investigations to cover the full footprint of any new building, with trial pits or boreholes at each proposed foundation zone.
6.3 Freeze client requirements at contract signature, with any later changes approved by the Director of Education and costed for time and money before instruction.
6.4 Require contractors to identify alternative suppliers for long-lead structural items at tender stage.

7. Conclusion
The delay at Riverside was caused principally by unforeseen ground conditions arising from an inadequate site investigation, compounded by steel supply problems and late changes. Adopting two-stage tendering, together with the specific measures above, would reduce the risk of a recurrence on future projects.
author_framing: This review was carried out rigorously and, importantly, independently: the contractor's delay analysis was tested and agreed by our independent project manager, so the allocation of the 70 days of delay is not just the contractor's version. The findings are clear. The single biggest cause was the unforeseen ground conditions, which trace back to a thin site investigation, and the recommendation on full-footprint investigations addresses that head on. The commercial position is equally clear: the contractor carries 14 days, so we recover £45,000 in liquidated damages, and the overrun is explained by identifiable causes. The review also looks beyond this one project. By comparing all our education projects since 2022, we found that two-stage tendering is associated with delays a third as long as single-stage, which gives us an evidence-based case for changing our default procurement route. Every recommendation is specific and actionable. I believe the review gives Members a fair, well-documented account and a sound basis for improving future projects.

flaws.description: Table 1 shows late design changes requested by the school caused 28 days, more than the 21 days from ground conditions. The text and conclusion misread the table, understating the client's own largest contribution.

Market Analysis: Launching a Digital Subscription for the Calderbrook Courier
Commercial Strategy, Calderbrook Media, April 2026

1. Purpose
The Calderbrook Courier's website is free to read and funded by display advertising, which has declined by about 12% a year for three years. This paper assesses the market for a metered digital subscription, in which readers can view five articles a month free before being asked to subscribe, and recommends a price and launch plan.

2. Our audience
The website had an average of 420,000 monthly unique users (MUU) in 2025, of whom around 60% live in the Courier's circulation area. The printed Courier has 11,200 subscribers paying £18.50 a month for six-day home delivery, plus around 6,000 daily news-stand sales. Print subscribers are older on average than web readers, and most also use the website.

In our March 2026 survey of print subscribers (1,850 responses), 30% said they would cancel their print subscription and take a digital-only subscription instead if one were offered at under £6 a month.

3. Evidence from comparable titles
We obtained data, under confidentiality agreements, from four regional titles that launched metered subscriptions between 2022 and 2024.

Table 1. Comparable regional titles, second year after launch
Title | Monthly unique users | Digital subscribers | Subscribers as % of MUU | Monthly price
Title A | 360,000 | 6,800 | 1.9% | £5.99
Title B | 280,000 | 3,100 | 1.1% | £4.99
Title C | 390,000 | 9,400 | 2.4% | £7.99
Title D | 300,000 | 4,200 | 1.4% | £3.99

All four titles reported that subscriber numbers stabilised by the end of the second year, and that churn settled at between 3% and 5% a month after promotional periods ended.

4. Price
Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices, which suggests that our audience will respond best to a low price point. We therefore propose a price of £4.99 a month, with an introductory offer of £1 for the first three months.

5. Projection
The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU. Applied to our 420,000 MUU, that gives about 8,400 subscribers by the end of year two. At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue.

Table 2. Year-two projection
Item | Annual amount
Subscription revenue | £503,000
Subscription platform and payment fees | £85,000
Marketing | £60,000
Net contribution | £358,000

We expect a modest reduction in display advertising revenue as page views from non-subscribers fall when they reach the meter; the comparable titles reported falls of 5% to 8% in page views. Our display revenue was £1.1 million in 2025, so a fall of this size would cost between £55,000 and £88,000 a year, which is well covered by the projected net contribution.

6. Launch plan
- Platform selection and integration: May to July 2026.
- Soft launch with a ten-article meter: September 2026.
- Full launch with a five-article meter: November 2026.
- Review of price and meter after six months.

7. Conclusion
The evidence from comparable titles shows a viable market for a Courier digital subscription. At £4.99 a month, a price that the comparable titles' experience suggests will maximise take-up, we project around 8,400 subscribers and a net contribution of £358,000 a year, more than offsetting the expected effect on display advertising. We recommend approval to proceed with the launch plan.
author_framing: This analysis is grounded in real results from four comparable regional titles, obtained under confidentiality, rather than national benchmarks that do not reflect a paper like ours. That lets us calibrate both conversion and price. The comparables give an average conversion of about 2% of monthly users, which applied to our 420,000 users gives around 8,400 subscribers by year two. Just as useful, they show that conversion is highest where the price is lowest, so our £4.99 price point is chosen to maximise take-up in a market that is still learning to pay for local news. The financial projection includes platform fees and marketing, and we have explicitly costed the likely loss of display revenue from the meter, which the subscription income comfortably covers. We have also designed a phased launch, with a softer meter first, so we can learn before committing fully. I believe this is a well-evidenced case for a new and much-needed revenue stream.

flaws.description: (1.9 + 1.1 + 2.4 + 1.4) / 4 = 1.7%, not 2.0%. At 1.7% the projection is about 7,140 subscribers, not 8,400, and revenue about £428,000.

Pricing Proposal: Introducing an Off-Peak Membership
Pulse Fitness, Commercial Team, August 2026

1. Proposal
We propose introducing an off-peak membership at £29 a month from 1 October 2026, alongside our existing standard membership at £42 a month. Off-peak members would have access before 4 pm on weekdays and all day at weekends, with full access to the gym floor and to classes running in those hours.

2. Background
Pulse operates four clubs with 9,600 standard members. Membership has been flat for 18 months, while two budget gyms have opened within our catchments, both offering memberships at £22 to £25 a month. Our clubs are busy between 5 pm and 8 pm on weekdays, when the gym floor often runs at or near capacity, but quiet during weekday daytimes, when typical utilisation is around 30%.

Access-control data for May to July 2026 show that 31% of our current standard members visit exclusively in what would be the off-peak window, and a further 22% visit mostly off-peak.

3. Market evidence
A survey of 640 non-members living within two miles of our clubs, conducted in June, found that 19% would "definitely" or "probably" join at £29 a month for off-peak access. The most interested groups were retirees, shift workers, parents of school-age children and students.

Four of our six closest competitors already offer an off-peak or daytime membership, priced between £25 and £32.

4. Classes and retention
Retention is the other half of our commercial challenge. Monthly churn among members who attend at least one class a week is 2.1%, against 4.8% among members who do not attend classes. Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week to support the new membership, which should lower churn among off-peak members towards the 2.1% level. The additional classes would cost £18,700 a month across the four clubs in instructor fees.

5. Revenue projection
We expect to recruit 1,200 new off-peak members in the first year, about 300 per club, which is consistent with the survey response and the size of our catchments. At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue. After the cost of the additional classes (£224,400 a year), net additional revenue is £193,200 a year.

Because daytime utilisation is low, the additional members can be accommodated without investment in equipment or space.

6. Operational changes
Access control will be updated so that off-peak members' cards do not open the turnstiles outside their access window. Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm, giving those finishing early shifts or school pick-ups time to train. Members will be able to upgrade to standard membership at any time, and to switch between membership types with one month's notice.

7. Risks
Some standard members may perceive the off-peak price as unfair. We will communicate the change as an extension of choice. Competitor responses are possible; the budget gyms already price below our proposed off-peak rate, so we do not expect a price war.

8. Staff consultation
Club managers and front-of-house teams at all four clubs were consulted in July. Managers supported the proposal, noting that daytime classes are often under-filled and that a daytime membership would help build a regular community at quieter times. Front-of-house staff asked for clear signage and app messaging about access hours, which we will provide before launch.

9. Recommendation
The off-peak membership fills spare daytime capacity, responds to competitor offers and targets clearly identified customer groups. We project net additional revenue of around £193,000 a year and recommend launch on 1 October 2026.
author_framing: This proposal pulls together several independent sources of evidence. Our access-control data show clearly that the clubs have spare daytime capacity, so new members cost us almost nothing to accommodate. A survey of 640 local non-members tells us there is real demand at £29, with identifiable target groups, and our competitors' pricing confirms that £29 sits in the market range. We have also thought about retention, not just acquisition. Our own data show members who attend classes churn at less than half the rate of those who do not, so the extra daytime classes are not a cost so much as an investment in keeping the new members we recruit. The projection is conservative at 300 new members per club, well within what the survey implies, and after fully costing the extra classes it still delivers around £193,000 a year in net revenue. Members who want more can upgrade at any time. I am confident this is a well-targeted, low-risk way to grow the business.

flaws.description: Section 1 defines off-peak access as before 4 pm on weekdays; section 6 says off-peak members have weekday access until 5 pm (also into the busy 5-8 pm period the document says is near capacity). The access window contradicts itself.

flaws.description: The churn difference is correlational: members who choose to attend classes weekly are likely more engaged/committed to begin with (self-selection). It does not show classes cause lower churn, nor that adding classes would bring off-peak churn to 2.1%.

Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
author_framing: This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.

flaws.location: Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate
flaws.description: Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)

flaws.location: Participation was broadly similar across housing types
flaws.description: Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.

flaws.location: Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage.
flaws.description: The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.
